questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A steady current of 5.0 A flows through a wire of uniform cross-sectional area 2.5 mm². The magnitude of the current density in the wire is:

solution.concept: Current density j = I/A
solution.explanation: Current density is the current per unit area of cross-section normal to the current. The area must be in m²: 2.5 mm² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁶ m².
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.0 A m⁻² leaves the area in mm². 5.0 × 10⁻⁷ A m⁻² divides the area by the current. 2.0 × 10³ A m⁻² converts mm² to m² with 10⁻³ instead of 10⁻⁶.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Ohm's law (current density)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The temperature coefficient of resistance of a metal, referred to 0 °C, is 5 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹ and may be taken as constant. A wire of this metal has resistance R₀ at 0 °C. The temperature at which its resistance becomes 1.5 R₀ is:

solution.concept: R_T = R₀[1 + α(T − T₀)]
solution.explanation: The resistance rises by the fraction αΔT. For a 50% rise, αΔT = 0.5.
solution.why_others_wrong: 300 °C uses αT = 1.5 (the whole ratio instead of the increase). 200 °C is the temperature at which the resistance doubles. 50 °C halves the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A cell of emf 2.0 V is connected across a 9.0 Ω resistor, and a current of 0.20 A flows in the circuit. The internal resistance of the cell is:

solution.concept: Circuit equation for a cell with internal resistance: I = ε/(R + r)
solution.explanation: The total resistance of the circuit is ε/I; the internal resistance is what remains after subtracting the external resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 Ω is the total resistance R + r. 0.20 Ω takes the lost voltage (0.2 V) as the resistance. 0.04 Ω multiplies the lost voltage by the current instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Three resistors of 2 Ω, 3 Ω and 6 Ω are connected in parallel across an ideal 6 V battery. The total current drawn from the battery is:

solution.concept: Parallel resistors: the same p.d. across each; currents add
solution.explanation: Each resistor has the full 6 V across it, so the currents are 3 A, 2 A and 1 A. Equivalently, 1/R = 1/2 + 1/3 + 1/6 = 1, so R = 1 Ω and I = 6 A.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.55 A treats the resistors as in series (11 Ω). 1 A is the current in the 6 Ω resistor alone. 11 A adds the resistances and multiplies instead of dividing.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The resistivity of an intrinsic semiconductor such as silicon decreases as its temperature rises. The main reason is that, with a rise in temperature:

options.text: the relaxation time of the charge carriers increases sharply
the charge carriers become heavier and so move more steadily
the number density of free charge carriers increases, more than making up for any decrease in the relaxation time
the band gap of the semiconductor increases

solution.concept: ρ = m/(ne²τ): resistivity depends on both n and τ
solution.explanation: In metals n is practically fixed and τ falls with temperature, so ρ rises. In semiconductors n rises steeply with temperature, and this more than compensates for any fall in τ, so ρ falls.
steps: Semiconductor: n increases rapidly with T → ρ decreases
solution.why_others_wrong: The relaxation time decreases (not increases) with temperature. The mass of the carriers does not change. A larger band gap would reduce, not increase, the number of carriers.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', temperature dependence of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option C: the number density of free charge carriers increases, more than making up for any decrease in the relaxation time

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: In a metal wire carrying a current, the drift speed of the free electrons (of the order of mm/s) is very much smaller than their random thermal speeds at room temperature (of the order of 10⁵ m/s).
Statement II: For a given electric field in a metal, the drift speed of the free electrons is directly proportional to their relaxation time.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Drift velocity v_d = eEτ/m superposed on random thermal motion
solution.explanation: Free electrons move randomly with speeds of about 10⁵ m/s; the field only adds a tiny average drift of about 1 mm/s (Statement I true). From v_d = eEτ/m, v_d ∝ τ for a given E (Statement II true).
steps: Thermal speeds ~10⁵ m/s ≫ drift speed ~10⁻³ m/s → I true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are NCERT results, so options with either statement false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A junction C in a circuit is connected to three points A, B and D by resistors of 2 Ω (C to A), 4 Ω (C to B) and 4 Ω (C to D). Nothing else is connected to C. The potentials of A, B and D are held at 10 V, 4 V and 0 V respectively. The potential of C is:

solution.concept: Kirchhoff's junction rule applied to a node
solution.explanation: No charge accumulates at C, so the currents into C from A, B and D add to zero: Σ(V_X − V_C)/R_X = 0.
steps: Multiply by 4: 20 − 2V + 4 − V − V = 0 → 4V = 24 → V = 6 V
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.67 V is the plain average of the three potentials, ignoring the resistances. 3.6 V weights each potential by its resistance instead of its conductance. 5 V has no basis in the junction rule.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Kirchhoff's rules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two resistors are placed in the two gaps of a metre bridge and the null point is found. When the two resistors are interchanged, the null point shifts along the wire by 20.0 cm. If the smaller resistance is 8 Ω, the larger resistance is:

solution.concept: Metre bridge balance R₁/R₂ = l/(100 − l); interchanging the resistors makes the null point 100 − l
solution.explanation: On interchanging, the null point moves from l to 100 − l, so the shift is 100 − 2l. A shift of 20 cm gives l = 40 cm for the smaller resistance's gap.
solution.why_others_wrong: 32 Ω takes the 20 cm shift itself as the balancing length (ratio 80 : 20). 10 Ω uses the ratio 50 : 40. 18 Ω squares the correct ratio.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge (metre bridge)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A uniform metal wire of resistance 4.0 Ω is stretched so that its length increases by 10%. Its volume, resistivity and temperature do not change. The percentage increase in its resistance is:

solution.concept: R = ρl/A with constant volume: A = V/l, so R = ρl²/V ∝ l²
solution.explanation: When the volume is fixed, stretching the wire also reduces its area in the same ratio, so the resistance grows as the square of the length.
solution.shortcut: For small stretches the increase is about 2 × 10% = 20%, but the exact value is 21%.
solution.why_others_wrong: 10% ignores the reduction in area. 20% is only the small-change approximation (2 × 10%). 33.1% uses R ∝ l³.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity of various materials

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A battery X (emf 10 V, internal resistance 1 Ω) is used to charge a battery Y (emf 6 V, internal resistance 1 Ω). The positive terminal of X is joined to the positive terminal of Y through a 2 Ω resistor, and the negative terminals are joined by a wire of negligible resistance. The rate at which electrical energy is converted into chemical energy in battery Y is:

solution.concept: Power stored in a battery being charged = ε × I; heat in its internal resistance is extra
solution.explanation: The emfs oppose each other in the loop, so the net emf is 10 − 6 = 4 V and the current is 4/(1 + 1 + 2) = 1 A. The part of the power that is stored chemically in Y is ε_Y × I; the I²r in Y is wasted as heat.
solution.why_others_wrong: 7 W is the total power delivered to Y, including the 1 W heat in its internal resistance. 10 W is the power generated by X. 4 W is the total heat produced in the circuit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A metal wire is connected across a battery that keeps a fixed potential difference between its ends. If the wire is heated, the drift speed of its free electrons increases.
Reason (R): The drift speed of the free electrons in a metal is given by v_d = eEτ/m, where τ is the relaxation time.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: v_d = eEτ/m; τ decreases as the temperature of a metal rises
solution.explanation: With a fixed p.d. and length, E is unchanged. Heating the metal makes the electrons collide more often, so τ decreases and v_d decreases. A is false. R is the correct expression for the drift speed, so R is true.
steps: Heating → more frequent collisions → τ decreases
v_d = eEτ/m decreases → A false; R true
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false because the drift speed falls, not rises; R is a correct NCERT relation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', drift of electrons and the origin of resistivity
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: If the cell and the galvanometer of a balanced Wheatstone bridge are interchanged, the bridge remains balanced.
Statement II: When a Wheatstone bridge is balanced, removing the galvanometer branch changes the current drawn from the cell.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Balance condition of a Wheatstone bridge, P/Q = R/S
solution.explanation: With the cell and galvanometer interchanged, the galvanometer joins the other pair of corners and the balance condition becomes P/R = Q/S, which is the same as P/Q = R/S (Statement I true). At balance no current flows in the galvanometer, so removing it changes no current in the circuit (Statement II false).
steps: Interchanged bridge: balance needs P/R = Q/S ⇔ P/Q = R/S → I true
At balance I_g = 0 → removing the galvanometer leaves all currents unchanged → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II is false because the galvanometer branch carries no current at balance; Statement I is true, so the remaining options are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', Wheatstone bridge
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two identical cells, each of emf ε and internal resistance r, and a resistor R are available. Match each arrangement in List-I with the current through R in List-II.

List-I:
A. One cell alone connected across R
B. Both cells in series (aiding each other), connected across R
C. Both cells in parallel (positive terminal to positive terminal), connected across R
D. Both cells in series but opposing each other (positive terminal joined to positive terminal), connected across R

List-II:
I. 2ε/(2R + r)
II. Zero
III. ε/(R + r)
IV. 2ε/(R + 2r)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Equivalent emf and internal resistance of series and parallel cells
solution.explanation: Series aiding: emf 2ε, internal resistance 2r → 2ε/(R + 2r). Parallel: emf ε, internal resistance r/2 → ε/(R + r/2) = 2ε/(2R + r). Series opposing: net emf zero → no current.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-III, B-I, C-IV swaps the series and parallel expressions. A-I/C-III swaps one cell with the parallel pair. C-II/D-I gives the opposing pair a current and the parallel pair none.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the resistivity of materials, as described in NCERT, are correct?

(a) Metals have low resistivities, in the range of about 10⁻⁸ Ω m to 10⁻⁶ Ω m.
(b) Semiconductors have resistivities lower than those of metals.
(c) The resistivity of nichrome is much greater than that of copper.
(d) The temperature coefficient of resistivity of nichrome is much smaller than that of copper.
(e) Near room temperature, the resistivity of germanium increases as its temperature rises.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Resistivity of metals, alloys and semiconductors and its temperature dependence
solution.explanation: Metals: 10⁻⁸–10⁻⁶ Ω m (a true). Semiconductors lie between metals and insulators, so their resistivity is higher than that of metals (b false). Nichrome (about 100 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m) is far more resistive than copper (1.7 × 10⁻⁸ Ω m) (c true), and its temperature coefficient (about 1.7 × 10⁻⁴ °C⁻¹) is much smaller than copper's (about 3.9 × 10⁻³ °C⁻¹) (d true). Germanium is a semiconductor, so its resistivity falls as temperature rises (e false).
steps: (b) false: semiconductors are more resistive than metals
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (b) or (e) include a false statement; (a) and (c) only leaves out the true statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', resistivity of various materials; temperature dependence of resistivity

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Two cells, of emf 2.0 V (internal resistance 0.50 Ω) and emf 1.5 V (internal resistance 0.25 Ω), are connected in series, aiding each other, across an external resistor R. The value of R for which the potential difference across the terminals of the 2.0 V cell is zero is:

solution.concept: Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir; a cell's terminal p.d. is zero when Ir = ε
solution.explanation: The 2.0 V cell has zero terminal p.d. when the current through it is ε/r = 4 A. The series circuit must then carry 4 A, which fixes R.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.875 Ω is the total resistance of the circuit, not R. 0.25 Ω equates R to the internal resistance of the other cell. 0.50 Ω equates R to the internal resistance of the 2.0 V cell.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: To measure a resistance R, a voltmeter of resistance 2400 Ω is connected directly across R, and an ammeter is connected in series with this combination. The voltmeter reads 4.8 V and the ammeter reads 0.050 A. The true value of R is:

solution.concept: The ammeter current divides between R and the voltmeter in parallel
solution.explanation: The ammeter reads the total current through R and the voltmeter. The voltmeter itself takes 4.8/2400 = 2 mA, so the current through R is 50 − 2 = 48 mA.
solution.why_others_wrong: 96 Ω is V/I, which ignores the current taken by the voltmeter. 92.3 Ω adds the voltmeter conductance instead of subtracting it. 2496 Ω treats the voltmeter as in series with R.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', combination of resistors - series and parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Twelve identical resistors, each of 12 Ω, form the edges of a cube. The equivalent resistance between two adjacent corners of the cube (the two ends of one edge) is:

solution.concept: Symmetry and Kirchhoff's rules in a resistor network; for an edge of a cube R_eq = 7R/12
solution.explanation: Feed current I in at corner A and out at the adjacent corner B. By symmetry, the current divides so that the direct edge AB carries 7I/12. Hence V_AB = (7I/12)R and R_eq = 7R/12.
steps: By symmetry, current in the direct edge AB = 7I/12
solution.why_others_wrong: 10 Ω (5R/6) is the resistance across a body diagonal. 9 Ω (3R/4) is the resistance across a face diagonal. 6 Ω treats the edge as two equal paths in parallel.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A bulb is connected across a battery whose internal resistance is not negligible. When a second, identical bulb is connected in parallel with the first, the first bulb becomes dimmer.
Reason (R): The potential difference across the terminals of a battery decreases as the current drawn from it increases, because V = ε − Ir.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Terminal voltage V = ε − Ir
solution.explanation: Adding a bulb in parallel lowers the external resistance, so the battery delivers a larger current. A larger current means a larger drop Ir inside the battery, so the terminal p.d. (which is the p.d. across each bulb) falls and the first bulb dims. R states exactly this mechanism.
steps: Second bulb in parallel → external resistance falls → I increases
P of first bulb = V²/R_bulb decreases → dimmer; R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true and the fall in terminal voltage is precisely why the first bulb dims, so R is the correct explanation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A cell of emf ε and internal resistance r is connected across an external resistor R. The efficiency of the cell is defined as the fraction of the power it generates that is delivered to R. The efficiency when the power delivered to R is maximum, and the efficiency when R = 3r, are respectively:

solution.concept: Efficiency η = I²R/[I²(R + r)] = R/(R + r); maximum power transfer at R = r
solution.explanation: The same current flows through R and r, so the fraction of power delivered to R is R/(R + r). Maximum power in R occurs at R = r, giving η = 1/2. For R = 3r, η = 3r/4r = 3/4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 100% would need r = 0. 25% is r/(R + r), the fraction wasted inside the cell. 75% and 50% reverses the two cases.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells, emf, internal resistance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Two identical cells, each of emf ε and internal resistance r, can be connected either in series (aiding) or in parallel (positive terminal to positive terminal) across an external resistor R. A single cell alone gives a current ε/(R + r). Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) If R is much larger than r, the series arrangement gives nearly twice the current of a single cell.
(b) If R is much smaller than r, the parallel arrangement gives nearly twice the current of a single cell.
(c) If R = r, the two arrangements give equal currents in R.
(d) In the parallel arrangement, the emf of the combination is 2ε.
(e) In the series arrangement, the internal resistance of the combination is r/2.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Series: emf 2ε, internal resistance 2r; parallel: emf ε, internal resistance r/2
solution.explanation: Series current 2ε/(R + 2r) → 2ε/R when R ≫ r, twice the single-cell value ε/R (a true). Parallel current 2ε/(2R + r) → 2ε/r when R ≪ r, twice ε/r (b true). With R = r both currents are 2ε/(3r) (c true). The emf of identical cells in parallel is ε, not 2ε (d false), and the series internal resistance is 2r, not r/2 (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) or (e) contain a false statement, and (a) and (b) only misses the true statement (c).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Current Electricity', cells in series and in parallel

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A small current element of length 2 mm carries a current of 5 A. Taking µ₀/4π = 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the magnetic field it produces at a point 10 cm away, the line joining the element to the point making an angle of 30° with the direction of the current, is:

solution.concept: Biot–Savart law: dB = (µ₀/4π) I dl sin θ / r²
solution.explanation: θ is the angle between the current element and the line joining it to the field point.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 × 10⁻⁷ T leaves out sin θ. 8.7 × 10⁻⁸ T uses cos 30° instead of sin 30°. 5 × 10⁻⁹ T divides by r instead of r².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field due to a current element, Biot–Savart law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A toroid has 500 turns wound uniformly on a ring of mean radius 10 cm, and carries a current of 1.0 A. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnetic field inside the core of the toroid (within the windings, at the mean radius) is:

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law for a toroid: B = µ₀NI/(2πr)
solution.explanation: A circular Amperian loop of radius r inside the core links all N turns, each carrying I, so B(2πr) = µ₀NI.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.3 × 10⁻³ T leaves out the 2π in the circumference. 1.6 × 10⁻³ T uses 4r instead of 2πr. Zero is the field in the open space inside or outside the toroid, not within the windings.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the toroid

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A particle of charge +2 µC moves with velocity 3 × 10⁴ m/s along the +x direction through a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T along the +y direction. The magnetic force on the particle is:

solution.concept: Magnetic (Lorentz) force F = q(v × B)
solution.explanation: The force is perpendicular to both v and B. With v along x̂ and B along ŷ, x̂ × ŷ = ẑ, and the charge is positive.
solution.why_others_wrong: −z is the direction for a negative charge (or for B × v). +y is along the field, but the magnetic force is always perpendicular to B. Zero would need v parallel to B.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long straight vertical wire carries a steady current upwards. At a point a short distance due east of the wire, the magnetic field due to the current points:

options.text: towards the east, away from the wire

solution.concept: Right-hand thumb rule for the field of a straight current
solution.explanation: Point the thumb of the right hand upwards along the current; the fingers curl anticlockwise as seen from above. At a point to the east of the wire, the anticlockwise circle is heading north.
steps: Field lines: horizontal circles round the wire, anticlockwise seen from above
Tangent at the east point of an anticlockwise circle points north
solution.why_others_wrong: South is the direction for a downward current. The field of a straight wire is perpendicular to the wire, so it cannot be vertical, and it is tangential to circles round the wire, not radial.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a straight wire / Ampere's circuital law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A rigid plane loop of wire of any shape carries a steady current and is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The loop:

options.text: experiences a net force along the field, but never a torque
experiences a net force perpendicular to the field and no torque
experiences zero net force, though it may experience a torque
experiences neither a force nor a torque in any orientation

solution.concept: Force on a closed current loop in a uniform field; torque τ = m × B
solution.explanation: The force on the loop is I(∮dl) × B, and ∮dl = 0 for a closed loop, so the net force in a uniform field is zero. The forces on different parts can still form a couple, giving a torque m × B unless m is parallel or antiparallel to B.
solution.why_others_wrong: A net force on a current loop needs a non-uniform field. Saying it never feels a torque contradicts τ = m × B (e.g. the moving-coil galvanometer).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', torque on current loop, magnetic dipole
solution.final_answer: Option C: experiences zero net force, though it may experience a torque

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The magnitude of the magnetic field due to a long straight wire carrying a steady current is inversely proportional to the distance from the wire.
Statement II: The magnetic field lines due to a long straight current-carrying wire are straight lines directed radially away from the wire.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Field of a long straight wire: B = µ₀I/(2πr), along circles round the wire
solution.explanation: B = µ₀I/(2πr), so B ∝ 1/r (Statement I true). The field lines are concentric circles in planes perpendicular to the wire, not radial lines (Statement II false).
steps: Field lines: concentric circles → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II describes the electric field of a line charge, not the magnetic field of a current.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A closed loop of wire consists of a quarter of a circle of radius 5 cm (centre O) together with the two straight radii joining the ends of the arc to O. A steady current of 10 A flows round the loop. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitude of the magnetic field at O is:

solution.concept: Field at the centre of an arc: B = (µ₀I/2R) × (θ/2π); straight segments pointing at O give no field there
solution.explanation: Each straight radius lies along a line through O, so for every element dl × r̂ = 0 and it contributes nothing. The quarter arc gives one quarter of the field at the centre of a full loop.
steps: Radial segments: dl ∥ r → zero field at O
solution.why_others_wrong: 4π × 10⁻⁵ T is the field of a complete loop. 2π × 10⁻⁵ T is that of a semicircle. 1 × 10⁻⁵ T has an extra factor π in the denominator.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic field on the axis of a circular current loop (centre)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A proton, a deuteron and an alpha particle, all having the same kinetic energy, enter a uniform magnetic field moving at right angles to it. Taking the masses in the ratio 1 : 2 : 4 and the charges in the ratio 1 : 1 : 2, the ratio of the radii of their circular paths, r_p : r_d : r_α, is:

solution.concept: r = mv/(qB) = √(2mK)/(qB); for the same K, r ∝ √m/q
solution.explanation: Writing the momentum in terms of kinetic energy, p = √(2mK), so at equal K the radius depends on √m/q.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 : 2 : 2 uses r ∝ m/q (equal speeds). 1 : √2 : √2 uses r ∝ √(m/q), which holds for equal accelerating potential differences, not equal kinetic energies. 1 : 1 : 1 ignores the masses.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A long coaxial cable consists of a thin central wire and a thin coaxial cylindrical sheath of radius 3 cm. The wire carries a steady current of 5 A along the axis, and the sheath carries 5 A back in the opposite direction. Taking µ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the magnitudes of the magnetic field at distances of 2 cm and 5 cm from the axis are, respectively:

solution.concept: Ampere's circuital law with circular Amperian loops: B(2πr) = µ₀I_enclosed
solution.explanation: At r = 2 cm the loop encloses only the central wire's 5 A. At r = 5 cm it encloses both currents, which cancel, so the net enclosed current and hence B (by symmetry) are zero.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 × 10⁻⁵ T at 5 cm ignores the return current in the sheath. Zero at 2 cm wrongly counts the sheath current inside a loop that does not enclose it. 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ T uses µ₀I/(4πr).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A flat circular coil of 50 turns, each of radius 10 cm, carries a current of 2.0 A. It is placed in a uniform magnetic field of 0.50 T so that the plane of the coil makes an angle of 60° with the direction of the field. The magnitude of the torque on the coil is about:

solution.concept: τ = NIAB sin θ, θ being the angle between the magnetic moment (normal to the coil) and B
solution.explanation: The magnetic moment is along the normal to the coil. If the plane makes 60° with B, the normal makes 30° with B.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.36 N m uses 60° as the angle between the moment and the field. 1.57 N m is the maximum torque (θ = 90°). 0.39 N m halves the correct value.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', torque on rectangular current loop in a uniform magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A moving-coil galvanometer has a coil resistance of 50 Ω and a figure of merit (current per division) of 4 µA per division, and its scale has 25 divisions on either side of zero. To convert it into a voltmeter of range 0–2 V, one should connect:

solution.concept: Full-scale current from the figure of merit; voltmeter: high resistance in series, I_g(G + R) = V
solution.explanation: Full-scale current I_g = 4 µA × 25 = 100 µA. For a full-scale reading at 2 V, the total resistance must be 2/(100 × 10⁻⁶) = 20 000 Ω, of which 50 Ω is the coil itself.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 000 Ω forgets to subtract the coil resistance. A resistance in parallel is a shunt, which converts the galvanometer into an ammeter. 1 950 Ω uses a full-scale current ten times too large.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the moving coil galvanometer

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field with its velocity inclined to the field. The pitch of its helical path does not depend on the component of its velocity perpendicular to the field.
Reason (R): The time taken by a charged particle to complete one revolution in a uniform magnetic field, 2πm/(qB), does not depend on its speed.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Helical motion: pitch p = v∥ T with T = 2πm/(qB)
solution.explanation: The pitch is the distance moved along the field during one revolution, p = v∥ × T. Because T = 2πm/(qB) is the same whatever the perpendicular speed, p depends only on v∥. R gives exactly this reason.
steps: So p is independent of v⊥; R explains A
solution.why_others_wrong: Both are true, and the speed-independence of the period is what makes the pitch independent of v⊥.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A steady current I flows in each arrangement. Match the location in List-I with the magnitude of the magnetic field there in List-II (n = turns per unit length, N = total turns, r = distance from the axis or centre, R = radius of the wire).

List-I:
A. Inside a long straight wire of radius R carrying current spread uniformly over its cross-section, at r < R
B. Within the windings (core) of a toroid of N turns, at distance r from its centre
C. Outside an ideal long solenoid, away from its ends
D. Well inside an ideal long solenoid

List-II:
I. µ₀nI
II. µ₀NI/(2πr)
III. µ₀Ir/(2πR²)
IV. Zero (practically)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Applications of Ampere's circuital law
solution.explanation: Inside the wire the enclosed current is I r²/R², so B = µ₀Ir/(2πR²). In the toroid core, B(2πr) = µ₀NI. Outside an ideal solenoid the field is practically zero; inside, B = µ₀nI.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II/B-III swaps the wire and toroid expressions. B-I/D-II swaps the toroid and solenoid. C-I/D-IV puts the uniform field outside the solenoid instead of inside.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', Ampere's circuital law; the solenoid; the toroid
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A moving-coil galvanometer is converted into an ammeter or into a voltmeter. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) An ammeter is made by connecting a low resistance (shunt) in parallel with the galvanometer.
(b) A voltmeter is made by connecting a high resistance in series with the galvanometer.
(c) An ideal ammeter has infinite resistance.
(d) The resistance of an ammeter made in this way is less than the resistance of its shunt.
(e) Connecting a series resistance to make a voltmeter increases the current sensitivity of the galvanometer.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Galvanometer as ammeter and voltmeter
solution.explanation: A shunt in parallel diverts most of the current (a true); a large series resistance limits the current for a given voltage (b true). An ideal ammeter has zero resistance so as not to change the current (c false). The parallel combination of G and S is smaller than S (d true). The current sensitivity NAB/k depends only on the galvanometer itself; a series resistance does not change it (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (c) or (e) contain a false statement, and (a) and (b) only leaves out the true statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the moving coil galvanometer

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A thin non-conducting ring of radius 10 cm carries a charge of 10 µC spread uniformly along it. It rotates about its own axis (the line through its centre perpendicular to its plane) at an angular speed of 100 rad/s. The magnetic dipole moment of the rotating ring is:

solution.concept: A rotating charge is a current I = q/T = qω/2π; magnetic moment m = IA
solution.explanation: The whole charge passes any point of the ring once per revolution, so the equivalent current is q/T = qω/(2π). This current circulates round an area πR².
solution.why_others_wrong: 1 × 10⁻⁵ A m² misses the factor ½ (uses I = qω/π). 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ A m² multiplies by R² but forgets the π of the area. 5 × 10⁻⁵ A m² uses R instead of R².
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', the magnetic dipole (current loop as a magnetic dipole)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A horizontal metal rod 0.50 m long and of mass 0.10 kg hangs from two light, flexible vertical conducting leads attached to its ends. A uniform vertical magnetic field of 0.50 T acts in the region, and a current of 2.0 A is passed through the rod. Taking g = 10 m/s², the rod swings aside and comes to rest with the leads inclined to the vertical at an angle of:

solution.concept: Force on a current-carrying conductor F = BIL; equilibrium of three forces
solution.explanation: The field is vertical and the rod horizontal, so the magnetic force BIL is horizontal. In equilibrium the leads' tension balances the resultant of the weight (vertical) and the magnetic force (horizontal).
solution.why_others_wrong: 30° takes sin θ = 0.5 instead of tan θ. tan⁻¹(2) inverts the ratio (mg/F). 45° assumes the two forces are equal.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force on a current-carrying conductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text: A proton (charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C) moves with velocity 2 × 10⁵ m/s along the +x direction through a region where there is a uniform electric field of 4 × 10⁴ V/m along +y and a uniform magnetic field of 0.1 T along +z. The net (Lorentz) force on the proton at that instant is:

solution.concept: Lorentz force F = q(E + v × B)
solution.explanation: The electric force qE is along +y. The magnetic force qv × B has x̂ × ẑ = −ŷ, so it is along −y. The two partly cancel; they would cancel completely only if v = E/B = 4 × 10⁵ m/s.
solution.why_others_wrong: 9.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ N takes the magnetic force along +y (wrong sign of x̂ × ẑ). −y reverses the larger, electric force. Zero assumes the fields balance, which needs v = E/B = 4 × 10⁵ m/s, not 2 × 10⁵ m/s.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', magnetic force (Lorentz force)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): Two identical charged particles move at right angles to the same uniform magnetic field, one with twice the speed of the other. The faster particle takes longer to complete one revolution.
Reason (R): The radius of the circular path of a charged particle moving at right angles to a uniform magnetic field is proportional to its speed.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: r = mv/(qB); T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB)
solution.explanation: The faster particle moves in a circle of twice the radius but at twice the speed, so its period 2πm/(qB) is the same: A is false. R (r ∝ v) is true.
steps: T = 2πr/v = 2πm/(qB), independent of v → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false because the period does not depend on speed; R is a true statement, so the key is 'A false, R true'.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
A charged particle (weight negligible) moves in the field region described in List-I. Match each case with the path or motion in List-II.

List-I:
A. Uniform electric field only; particle released from rest
B. Uniform magnetic field only; velocity perpendicular to the field
C. Uniform magnetic field only; velocity at an acute angle to the field
D. Uniform electric and magnetic fields perpendicular to each other; velocity perpendicular to both and of magnitude E/B, in the direction for which the two forces are opposite

List-II:
I. Helix with its axis along the field
II. Straight line with constant velocity
III. Straight line with uniform acceleration
IV. Circle traversed at constant speed

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Motion of charges in electric and magnetic fields; velocity selector
solution.explanation: From rest in a uniform E, the constant force qE gives uniformly accelerated straight-line motion. A uniform B perpendicular to v gives uniform circular motion. With an acute angle, the parallel component is unaffected, so the path is a helix. In crossed fields with v = E/B the forces qE and qvB cancel, so the particle goes straight at constant velocity.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV/B-III swaps the electric-field and magnetic-field motions. B-I/C-IV swaps the circle and the helix. A-II/D-III swaps the uniformly accelerated and the undeflected motions.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in combined electric and magnetic fields (velocity selector)
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Magnetic Effects of Current and Magnetism
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about magnetic materials are correct?

(a) The individual atoms of a paramagnetic substance possess permanent magnetic dipole moments.
(b) In a weak field at room temperature, the atomic dipoles of a paramagnetic substance line up completely along the field.
(c) In a diamagnetic substance placed in a magnetic field, the electron orbits are modified so as to produce a net magnetic moment opposite to the field.
(d) A superconductor expels a magnetic field completely from its interior (the Meissner effect).
(e) The relative permeability of a superconductor is 1.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Microscopic picture of para- and diamagnetism; superconductors as perfect diamagnets
solution.explanation: Paramagnetic atoms have permanent dipole moments (a true), but thermal agitation keeps them largely random; only strong fields at low temperatures approach full alignment (b false). Diamagnetism arises from induced moments opposite to the field (c true). Superconductors are perfect diamagnets: the field is expelled (d true), χ = −1, so µ_r = 1 + χ = 0, not 1 (e false).
steps: (b) false: thermal agitation prevents full alignment
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (b) or (e) include a false statement, and (a) and (c) only misses the true statement (d).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Magnetism and Matter', magnetic properties of materials

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A single-turn conducting loop of area 0.05 m² and resistance 2 Ω lies with its plane perpendicular to a uniform magnetic field. The field is reduced uniformly from 0.4 T to zero in 0.02 s. The current induced in the loop during this time is:

solution.concept: Faraday's law ε = |ΔΦ|/Δt; Ohm's law I = ε/R
solution.explanation: The flux falls from BA to zero at a steady rate, so the emf is constant during the change.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.0 A takes the emf (in volts) as the current. 2.0 A multiplies the emf by R. 0.01 A divides the flux change by R but forgets to divide by the time.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Faraday's law of induction

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A steady current of 2.0 A in coil 1 produces a total magnetic flux linkage of 4.0 × 10⁻³ Wb with a nearby coil 2. The mutual inductance of the pair of coils is:

solution.concept: Mutual inductance: N₂Φ₂ = M I₁
solution.explanation: The flux linkage of coil 2 is proportional to the current in coil 1; the constant of proportionality is M.
solution.why_others_wrong: 8.0 mH multiplies the flux linkage by the current. 4.0 mH ignores the current. 500 H divides the current by the flux linkage.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance - mutual inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A rectangular conducting loop lies in the plane of the page, partly inside a region of uniform magnetic field directed into the page. The loop is pulled out of the field region at constant velocity. As seen by a reader looking at the page, the current induced in the loop while it is leaving the field is:

options.text: zero, because the loop moves at constant velocity
clockwise in one half of the loop and anticlockwise in the other

solution.concept: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the change in flux
solution.explanation: As the loop leaves the field, the flux into the page through it decreases. The induced current tries to maintain this flux, so it produces a field into the page inside the loop; by the right-hand rule, that is a clockwise current as seen by the reader.
steps: Induced field: into the page inside the loop
solution.why_others_wrong: Anticlockwise would increase the decrease in flux, violating Lenz's law. Constant velocity still changes the flux, so there is an emf. A single loop carries one current all the way round.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', Lenz's law and conservation of energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For an ideal transformer, the ratio of the secondary voltage to the primary voltage equals the ratio of the number of turns in the secondary to that in the primary.
Statement II: The frequency of the alternating emf produced by an AC generator equals the number of rotations made by its coil per second.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Transformer equation V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p; AC generator emf ε = NBAω sin ωt
solution.explanation: In an ideal transformer each turn has the same emf, so V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p (Statement I true). In a generator the emf goes through one complete cycle for each rotation of the coil, so ν = ω/2π is the number of rotations per second (Statement II true).
steps: ε = ε₀ sin ωt, ω = 2πν → one cycle per rotation → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are standard NCERT results, so the options calling either false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', AC generator; Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', transformers
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An alternating voltage is given by v = 200 sin(100πt), with v in volts and t in seconds. The least time after t = 0 at which the instantaneous voltage becomes 100 V is:

solution.concept: Instantaneous value v = v₀ sin ωt
solution.explanation: Setting v = v₀/2 gives sin ωt = 1/2, whose smallest positive solution is ωt = π/6.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1/300 s uses ωt = π/3 (where sin = √3/2). 1/200 s is the time to reach the peak (ωt = π/2). 1/1200 s uses ωt = π/12.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to a resistor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal inductor of inductance 0.20 H (no resistance) is connected in series with a 4 Ω resistor across a battery of emf 12 V and internal resistance 2 Ω. Long after the circuit is closed, the energy stored in the magnetic field of the inductor is:

solution.concept: Steady DC: an ideal inductor has no p.d. across it; magnetic energy U = ½LI²
solution.explanation: Once the current is steady, dI/dt = 0, so the ideal inductor behaves as a plain wire and the current is fixed by the resistances. The inductor still stores energy ½LI² because a current flows through it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.8 J forgets the factor ½. 0.9 J ignores the internal resistance (I = 3 A). Zero confuses the absence of a self-induced emf with the absence of stored energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance - self-inductance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An ideal step-up transformer has a turns ratio N_p : N_s = 1 : 20. Its primary is connected to a 230 V AC supply and its secondary to a 2300 Ω resistive load. The currents in the secondary and in the primary are, respectively:

solution.concept: V_s/V_p = N_s/N_p; ideal transformer: V_p I_p = V_s I_s
solution.explanation: The secondary voltage is 20 × 230 = 4600 V, which drives 2 A through the load. Since no power is lost, the primary current is 20 times the secondary current.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.1 A for the primary makes the current step up with the voltage (violating energy conservation). 40 A and 2 A swaps the two currents. 0.1 A for the secondary uses 230 V across the load.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', transformers

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: At a frequency of 50 Hz, a certain capacitor has a reactance of 100 Ω and a certain inductor has a reactance of 25 Ω. If the two are connected in series with a resistor, the circuit will be in resonance at a frequency of:

solution.concept: X_L = ωL ∝ f, X_C = 1/(ωC) ∝ 1/f; resonance when X_L = X_C
solution.explanation: Raising the frequency by a factor k multiplies X_L by k and divides X_C by k. They become equal when 25k = 100/k, i.e. k² = 4.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 Hz takes k = 4 (forgetting the square root). 25 Hz lowers the frequency, which makes X_C even larger. 12.5 Hz uses k = 1/4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit - resonance

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For a long air-cored solenoid of fixed length and cross-section, the self-inductance is proportional to the square of the number of turns per unit length.
Reason (R): The self-induced emf in a coil always opposes the change in the current through it.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: L = µ₀n²Al for a long solenoid; Lenz's law for self-induction
solution.explanation: Doubling n doubles the field B = µ₀nI and also doubles the number of turns it links, so L = µ₀n²Al (A true). R is also true (Lenz's law), but it describes the direction of the self-induced emf, not why L depends on n²; it does not explain A.
steps: Flux linkage NΦ = (nl)(µ₀nI)A → L = µ₀n²Al → A true
R concerns the sign of the emf, not the n² dependence → not the explanation
solution.why_others_wrong: R is true but is about the direction of the induced emf; the n² dependence comes from n appearing both in the field and in the number of turns linked.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', inductance - self-inductance
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each source of energy loss in a practical transformer (List-I) with the way it is reduced (List-II), as described in NCERT.

List-I:
A. Flux leakage
B. Resistance of the windings
C. Eddy currents in the iron core
D. Hysteresis (repeated magnetisation and demagnetisation of the core)

List-II:
I. Using a laminated core
II. Using a core material with a low hysteresis loss
III. Winding the primary and secondary coils one over the other
IV. Using thick wire for windings carrying large currents

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Energy losses in transformers
solution.explanation: Leakage is reduced by winding the coils over each other so that they share the flux. Joule heating in the windings is reduced by thick (low-resistance) wire. Eddy currents are reduced by laminating the core. Hysteresis loss is reduced by choosing a core material with a low hysteresis loss.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV/B-III swaps leakage and winding resistance. C-II/D-I swaps the eddy-current and hysteresis remedies. A-I/C-III swaps leakage and eddy currents.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', transformers
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A series LCR circuit with R = 30 Ω is at resonance when driven at a frequency f₀; at this frequency the inductive and capacitive reactances are each 20 Ω. The source frequency is now changed to 2f₀, all components unchanged. The impedance of the circuit becomes:

solution.concept: X_L ∝ f, X_C ∝ 1/f; Z = √[R² + (X_L − X_C)²]
solution.explanation: At 2f₀ the inductive reactance doubles to 40 Ω and the capacitive reactance halves to 10 Ω.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 Ω is the impedance at resonance. 60 Ω adds R and (X_L − X_C) arithmetically instead of in quadrature. About 58 Ω adds the two reactances instead of subtracting them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', series LCR circuit

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A long straight wire carries a steady current of 10 A. A rectangular conducting loop lies in the same plane, with two of its sides, each 0.20 m long, parallel to the wire; at a certain instant these sides are 0.10 m and 0.40 m from the wire. The loop moves directly away from the wire with a speed of 5.0 m/s. Taking µ₀/2π = 2 × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹, the emf induced in the loop at this instant is:

solution.concept: Motional emf Blv in each side parallel to the wire; B = µ₀I/(2πx)
solution.explanation: The two sides perpendicular to the wire move along their own length and have no motional emf. The two parallel sides each have an emf Blv, but they are in opposite senses round the loop, so the net emf is the difference.
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 µV counts only the near side. 25 µV adds the two emfs although they oppose each other round the loop. 5 µV counts only the far side.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', motional electromotive force

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When an ideal inductor is connected to an AC source, the average power over a complete cycle is zero, although the instantaneous power is non-zero at most instants.
Statement II: When an ideal inductor is connected to an AC source, the instantaneous power delivered to it is positive at every instant.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Power in a purely inductive circuit: p = vi with i lagging v by π/2
solution.explanation: With i lagging v by π/2, p = v₀i₀ sin ωt sin(ωt − π/2) = −½v₀i₀ sin 2ωt. It is non-zero except at isolated instants and averages to zero (Statement I true). It is negative for half the time, when the inductor returns its stored energy to the source (Statement II false).
steps: Average over a cycle = 0 → I true
p < 0 for half of each cycle → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II ignores the quarter-cycles in which the inductor gives back the energy stored in its field.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Alternating Current', AC voltage applied to an inductor
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
The coil of an AC generator, having N turns each of area A, rotates with a constant angular speed ω in a uniform magnetic field B, about an axis perpendicular to the field. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The magnetic flux through the coil is maximum at the instants when the induced emf is zero.
(b) The induced emf is given by ε = NBAω sin ωt, taking the coil's plane perpendicular to B at t = 0.
(c) Doubling the number of turns, everything else unchanged, doubles the peak emf.
(d) The frequency of the induced emf depends on the strength of the magnetic field.
(e) In hydroelectric generators, the coil is rotated by water falling from a height.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: AC generator: Φ = NBA cos ωt, ε = NBAω sin ωt
solution.explanation: Φ = NBA cos ωt is maximum when sin ωt = 0, i.e. when ε = 0 (a true). ε = −dΦ/dt = NBAω sin ωt (b true). The peak emf NBAω is proportional to N (c true). The frequency is ω/2π, set by the rotation rate, not by B (d false). NCERT notes that in hydroelectric generators the falling water rotates the coil (e true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) include a false statement; (a), (b) and (c) only and (b), (c) and (e) only each leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Induction', AC generator

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Infrared waves are sometimes referred to as heat waves. According to NCERT, this is because:

options.text: infrared waves travel faster than visible light in vacuum
infrared waves are produced only by bodies at very high temperatures, such as the Sun
infrared waves carry electric charge that heats the material they fall on
water molecules present in most materials readily absorb infrared waves, which increases their thermal motion and so heats the material

solution.concept: Infrared radiation and its heating effect
solution.explanation: Many molecules, especially water, absorb infrared strongly. The absorbed energy increases their thermal motion, raising the temperature of the material.
steps: Infrared is absorbed by water molecules
solution.why_others_wrong: All electromagnetic waves travel at c in vacuum. Infrared is emitted by hot bodies and molecules generally, not only very hot ones. Electromagnetic waves carry no charge.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum - infrared waves
solution.final_answer: Option D: water molecules present in most materials readily absorb infrared waves, which increases their thermal motion and so heats the material

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The magnetic field of a plane electromagnetic wave in vacuum is B_y = 2 × 10⁻⁷ sin(0.5 × 10³ x + 1.5 × 10¹¹ t) T, with x in metres and t in seconds. Taking c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s, the amplitude of the electric field of the wave and its direction of propagation are:

solution.concept: E₀ = cB₀; a wave sin(kx + ωt) travels towards −x
solution.explanation: The amplitudes are related by E₀ = cB₀. The phase kx + ωt stays constant if x decreases as t increases, so the wave travels along −x. (Check: ω/k = 1.5 × 10¹¹/0.5 × 10³ = 3 × 10⁸ m/s = c.)
solution.why_others_wrong: +x is the direction for sin(kx − ωt). 6.7 × 10⁻¹⁶ V/m divides B₀ by c instead of multiplying. The wave cannot travel along y, the direction of its own magnetic field.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic waves

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: While a capacitor is being charged, the electric flux through a surface between its plates increases at the rate of 4.0 × 10⁸ V m s⁻¹. Taking ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C² N⁻¹ m⁻², the displacement current through that surface is about:

options.text: zero, since no charge crosses the gap

solution.concept: Displacement current i_d = ε₀ dΦ_E/dt
solution.explanation: Maxwell's displacement current is ε₀ times the rate of change of electric flux. It exists even though no charge flows across the gap.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.5 × 10¹⁹ A divides by ε₀ instead of multiplying. 3.5 A is off by a factor of 1000. Zero ignores the displacement current, which is exactly what keeps the total current continuous.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', displacement current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each part of the electromagnetic spectrum in List-I with its approximate wavelength range in List-II, as given in NCERT.

List-I:
A. Radio waves
B. Microwaves
C. Infrared
D. Ultraviolet

List-II:
I. 400 nm to 1 nm
II. 1 mm to 700 nm
III. > 0.1 m
IV. 0.1 m to 1 mm

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Wavelength ranges of the electromagnetic spectrum
solution.explanation: In order of decreasing wavelength: radio waves (> 0.1 m), microwaves (0.1 m to 1 mm), infrared (1 mm to 700 nm), visible light (700 nm to 400 nm), ultraviolet (400 nm to 1 nm), X-rays and gamma rays.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-IV/B-III swaps radio waves and microwaves. C-I/D-II swaps infrared and ultraviolet across the visible band. B-II/C-IV swaps microwaves and infrared.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Electromagnetic Waves', electromagnetic spectrum (Table 8.1)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object 3.0 cm tall stands on the principal axis of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 40 cm, 60 cm in front of the mirror. The size and nature of the image are:

solution.concept: f = R/2; mirror formula 1/v + 1/u = 1/f; m = −v/u
solution.explanation: With the Cartesian sign convention, f = −20 cm and u = −60 cm (object beyond C), so a real, inverted, diminished image forms between F and C.
solution.why_others_wrong: Erect contradicts the negative magnification of a real image. 6.0 cm takes f = R = 40 cm. 0.75 cm uses m = 1/4.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', the mirror equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An object is placed 30 cm in front of a thin concave lens of focal length 15 cm. The image formed is:

options.text: 30 cm from the lens on the other side; real, inverted and of the same size as the object
10 cm from the lens on the same side as the object; virtual, erect and one-third the size of the object
10 cm from the lens on the other side; real, inverted and one-third the size of the object
30 cm from the lens on the same side; virtual, erect and of the same size as the object

solution.concept: Thin lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f; m = v/u
solution.explanation: For a concave lens f = −15 cm; with u = −30 cm, the image is virtual and on the object side, as always for a concave lens with a real object.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30 cm on the other side, same size, is the result for a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. A concave lens cannot form a real image of a real object. 30 cm on the same side ignores the lens formula.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', thin lens formula
solution.final_answer: Option B: 10 cm from the lens on the same side as the object; virtual, erect and one-third the size of the object

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin prism of refracting angle 4° is made of glass of refractive index 1.5. The deviation it produces in a ray of light passing through it (at near-normal incidence) is:

solution.concept: Deviation by a thin prism: δ = (n − 1)A
solution.explanation: For a thin prism and small angles, the minimum deviation reduces to δ = (n − 1)A.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6° uses nA instead of (n − 1)A. 2.7° divides A by n. 1° has an extra factor ½.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Plane-polarised light of intensity 8.0 W m⁻² falls normally on an ideal polaroid whose pass axis makes an angle of 60° with the direction of vibration of the electric field of the light. The intensity of the transmitted light is:

solution.concept: Malus' law: I = I₀ cos² θ
solution.explanation: Only the component of E along the pass axis, E₀ cos θ, is transmitted; intensity goes as the square of the amplitude.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4.0 W m⁻² uses cos θ instead of cos² θ. 6.0 W m⁻² uses sin² θ. 1.0 W m⁻² halves again, as if the incident light were unpolarised.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A polaroid consists of long-chain molecules aligned in a particular direction. When unpolarised light falls on it, according to NCERT:

options.text: the electric vectors perpendicular to the aligned molecules are absorbed, so the pass axis is along the molecules
the light is reflected from the molecules, which polarises it
the electric vectors along the direction of the aligned molecules are absorbed, so the pass axis is perpendicular to the molecules
all the electric vectors are transmitted, but their frequency is halved

solution.concept: Working of a polaroid
solution.explanation: The long-chain molecules absorb the component of the electric field parallel to their length. The component perpendicular to them is transmitted, so the pass axis is perpendicular to the aligned molecules.
solution.why_others_wrong: The second option reverses absorption and transmission. A polaroid works by selective absorption, not reflection. Polarisation never changes the frequency of light.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', polarisation
solution.final_answer: Option C: the electric vectors along the direction of the aligned molecules are absorbed, so the pass axis is perpendicular to the molecules

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A convex mirror is preferred as a rear-view mirror in vehicles mainly because, for real objects behind the vehicle, it:

options.text: always forms an erect, diminished image and so gives a wider field of view
forms a real, inverted image that can be seen on a screen
forms a magnified image of nearby vehicles
forms an image at the same distance as the object, like a plane mirror

solution.concept: Image formation by a convex mirror
solution.explanation: A convex mirror forms a virtual, erect, diminished image of every real object, between the pole and the focus. Because the images are smaller, a much wider region behind the vehicle can be seen in a small mirror.
steps: Convex mirror: virtual, erect, diminished images
Diminished images → wide field of view
solution.why_others_wrong: A convex mirror never forms a real image of a real object. Its images are diminished, not magnified. Image distance equal to object distance describes a plane mirror.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', reflection of light by spherical mirrors
solution.final_answer: Option A: always forms an erect, diminished image and so gives a wider field of view

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When light from two independent (incoherent) sources, each producing intensity I₀ at a point, superposes there, the resultant intensity is 2I₀.
Statement II: With two such incoherent sources, a stationary pattern of bright and dark fringes is seen on a screen, with the intensity varying between 0 and 4I₀.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Coherent and incoherent addition of light waves
solution.explanation: For incoherent sources the phase difference changes rapidly and randomly, so cos φ averages to zero and the intensities simply add: I = 2I₀ (Statement I true). For the same reason no stationary fringes are formed; the screen is uniformly illuminated (Statement II false).
steps: I = I₁ + I₂ + 2√(I₁I₂)⟨cos φ⟩, ⟨cos φ⟩ = 0 → 2I₀ → I true
No stable φ → no stationary fringes → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II describes coherent sources; with incoherent sources the intensity is uniform at 2I₀.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', coherent and incoherent addition of waves
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin biconvex lens made of glass of refractive index 1.5 has a focal length of 20 cm in air. It is completely immersed in a transparent liquid of refractive index 1.75. Its focal length in the liquid is:

options.text: −70 cm (it behaves as a diverging lens)

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula with relative refractive index: 1/f = (n_g/n_m − 1)(1/R₁ − 1/R₂)
solution.explanation: The curvature factor is the same in air and in the liquid, so the focal lengths are in the inverse ratio of (n_g/n_m − 1). In a liquid denser than the glass, this factor is negative and the lens diverges.
solution.why_others_wrong: +70 cm ignores the change of sign: the liquid is optically denser than the glass. −20 cm just reverses the sign. +80 cm is the value for water (n = 4/3), which is less dense than the glass.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction at spherical surfaces and by lenses (lens-maker's formula)
solution.final_answer: Option B: −70 cm (it behaves as a diverging lens)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A ray of light passes through an equilateral glass prism (refracting angle 60°) of refractive index √3 in the position of minimum deviation. The angle of incidence on the first face and the angle of minimum deviation are, respectively:

solution.concept: At minimum deviation r₁ = r₂ = A/2, i = e, and D_m = 2i − A
solution.explanation: At minimum deviation the ray passes symmetrically, so each refraction angle inside is A/2 = 30°. Snell's law at the first face then gives i.
solution.why_others_wrong: 30° is the angle of refraction inside the prism, not the angle of incidence. D_m = 30° uses D_m = i − A/2. 45° would need n = √2.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction through a prism

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: An astronomical telescope has an objective of focal length 150 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5.0 cm, and is used in normal adjustment. The Moon subtends an angle of 0.5° at the unaided eye. The angle subtended at the eye by the final image of the Moon is about:

solution.concept: Angular magnification of a telescope in normal adjustment: m = f_o/f_e = β/α
solution.explanation: Magnifying power is defined as the ratio of the angle subtended by the final image to the angle subtended by the object at the unaided eye; for small angles, β = mα.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.017° divides the angle by m instead of multiplying. 0.5° ignores the magnification. 7.5° halves the magnification.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments - telescope

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Light of wavelength 600 nm falls normally on a single slit of width 0.30 mm, and the diffraction pattern is observed on a screen 1.5 m away. Using the approximate condition for the secondary maxima, θ ≈ (n + ½)λ/a, the distance of the first secondary maximum from the centre of the pattern is about:

solution.concept: Single-slit pattern: minima at θ = nλ/a, secondary maxima approximately at θ = (n + ½)λ/a
solution.explanation: The first secondary maximum lies roughly midway between the first and second minima, at θ ≈ 3λ/(2a). On the screen, y = Dθ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.0 mm is the position of the first minimum (λ/a). 6.0 mm is that of the second minimum (2λ/a). 2.25 mm uses λ/(2a).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction - the single slit

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In Young's double-slit experiment, the bright fringes near the centre of the pattern are equally spaced.
Reason (R): In the diffraction pattern of a single slit, all the secondary maxima have the same intensity as the central maximum.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Fringe positions in Young's experiment; intensity distribution in single-slit diffraction
solution.explanation: For small angles the nth bright fringe is at x = nλD/d, so successive fringes are a constant β = λD/d apart (A true). In single-slit diffraction the central maximum is much the brightest and the secondary maxima become weaker with increasing order (R false).
steps: x_n = nλD/d → equal spacing β → A true
Secondary maxima much weaker than the central one → R false
solution.why_others_wrong: R is false, so the options treating R as true are wrong; A is true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment; diffraction
solution.final_answer: Option C: A is true but R is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
In a Young's double-slit experiment (with the slit separation, screen distance and wavelength initially fixed) and in a single-slit diffraction experiment, one change is made at a time, as in List-I. Match each change with its effect in List-II.

List-I:
A. Young's experiment: the wavelength is changed from 600 nm to 400 nm (fringe width)
B. Young's experiment: the distance of the screen from the slits is doubled (fringe width)
C. Single slit: the slit width is doubled (linear width of the central maximum)
D. Young's experiment: the whole apparatus is immersed in water of refractive index 4/3 (fringe width)

List-II:
I. Becomes 3/4 of its value
II. Becomes half
III. Becomes double
IV. Becomes 2/3 of its value

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Fringe width β = λD/d; central maximum width 2λD/a; λ in a medium = λ/n
solution.explanation: β ∝ λ: 400/600 = 2/3. β ∝ D: doubled. Central maximum ∝ 1/a: halved. In water the wavelength becomes λ/n = 3λ/4, so β becomes 3/4.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I/D-IV swaps the wavelength and immersion effects. B-II/C-III inverts both dependences. C-I/D-II gives the slit-width change the water effect.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', interference of light waves and Young's experiment; diffraction
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-IV, B-III, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Using the Cartesian sign convention for spherical mirrors (distances measured from the pole, positive in the direction of the incident light), which of the following statements are correct?

(a) The focal length of a concave mirror is negative.
(b) The magnification of a real image formed by a spherical mirror is negative.
(c) The mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f applies to both concave and convex mirrors.
(d) For a real object, the image distance for a convex mirror is positive.
(e) A convex mirror can form a real image of a real object.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Sign convention for spherical mirrors
solution.explanation: Light is incident from the left, so distances in front of the mirror are negative: a concave mirror's focus is in front (a true), and a real image is in front and inverted, giving m = −v/u < 0 (b true). The mirror equation holds for both kinds with signs (c true). A convex mirror's virtual image is behind the mirror, so v > 0 (d true); it never forms a real image of a real object (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (e) include a false statement; the others leave out at least one true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', sign convention; the mirror equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: For a compound microscope with given objective and tube length, using an eyepiece of shorter focal length increases the magnifying power.
Statement II: For an astronomical telescope in normal adjustment, using an eyepiece of longer focal length, the objective being unchanged, increases the magnifying power.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Microscope m ≈ (L/f_o)(D/f_e); telescope m = f_o/f_e
solution.explanation: In both instruments the eyepiece magnification is inversely proportional to f_e. A shorter f_e increases the microscope's magnifying power (Statement I true), and a longer f_e reduces the telescope's magnifying power f_o/f_e (Statement II false).
steps: Telescope: m = f_o/f_e → larger f_e gives smaller m → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II reverses the dependence on the eyepiece focal length.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', optical instruments
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A thin convex lens of focal length 20 cm has a plane mirror placed 40 cm behind it, perpendicular to its principal axis. A point object is on the axis 30 cm in front of the lens. After refraction through the lens, reflection at the mirror and refraction through the lens again, the final image is formed:
