options.text: 20 cm in front of the lens
at the object itself, 30 cm in front of the lens
at infinity: the light emerges from the lens as a parallel beam

solution.concept: Successive image formation; a converging beam on a plane mirror acts as a virtual object
solution.explanation: The lens alone would form an image 60 cm behind it, i.e. 20 cm behind the mirror. The mirror reflects the converging rays so that they meet 20 cm in front of the mirror, which is 20 cm from the lens. This point is at the focus of the lens, so the returning light emerges parallel.
steps: Virtual object 20 cm behind the mirror → image 20 cm in front
That point is 40 − 20 = 20 cm from the lens = f → emergent beam parallel
solution.why_others_wrong: 20 cm in front of the lens forgets the second refraction. Returning to the object would need the mirror at the lens's image point (60 cm). 60 cm behind the lens ignores the mirror.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens; reflection by mirrors
solution.final_answer: Option D: at infinity: the light emerges from the lens as a parallel beam

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small air bubble is inside a solid glass sphere of radius 10 cm and refractive index 1.5, at a distance of 5 cm from the surface along a radius (i.e. halfway between the surface and the centre). Viewed from outside along that radius, from the side nearer the bubble, the bubble appears to be below the surface at a depth of:

solution.concept: Refraction at a spherical surface: n₂/v − n₁/u = (n₂ − n₁)/R
solution.explanation: Light goes from glass (n₁ = 1.5) to air (n₂ = 1). Taking the direction of the emerging light as positive, the object (bubble) is at u = −5 cm and the centre of curvature is on the glass side, so R = −10 cm.
steps: The image is 4.0 cm inside the glass from the surface
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.3 cm uses the plane-surface formula (real depth/n). 2.9 cm takes R with the wrong sign. 5.0 cm ignores refraction.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction at spherical surfaces

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A single slit is illuminated normally by light containing two wavelengths. The first minimum of the diffraction pattern of the 600 nm light falls at the same angle as the first secondary maximum of the other wavelength. Taking the secondary maxima at sin θ ≈ (n + ½)λ/a, the other wavelength is:

solution.concept: Single slit: first minimum a sin θ = λ; first secondary maximum a sin θ ≈ 3λ/2
solution.explanation: Equating the two path-difference conditions at the same angle: λ₁ = (3/2)λ₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 900 nm multiplies by 1.5 instead of dividing. 300 nm uses the second minimum condition (2λ₂). 600 nm assumes the minimum and maximum coincide for the same wavelength.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Wave Optics', diffraction - the single slit

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A small object lies on the principal axis of a concave mirror of focal length 20 cm, 30 cm in front of it, and moves along the axis towards the mirror at 2 cm/s. At this instant the image moves:

options.text: at 4 cm/s, away from the mirror
at 8 cm/s, away from the mirror

solution.concept: Differentiating the mirror equation: dv/dt = −(v²/u²) du/dt = −m² du/dt
solution.explanation: From 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, −(1/v²)dv/dt − (1/u²)du/dt = 0. The image speed is m² times the object speed, in the opposite sense along the axis. As the object moves from 30 cm towards F, the real image moves out towards infinity, away from the mirror.
steps: u → F makes |v| increase → image moves away from the mirror
solution.why_others_wrong: Towards the mirror reverses the direction (the image recedes as the object approaches F). 4 cm/s uses |m| instead of m². 2 cm/s assumes the image moves like the object.
solution.final_answer: Option C: at 8 cm/s, away from the mirror

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): A ray of light falling normally on one refracting face of an equilateral glass prism of refractive index 1.5 emerges from the second refracting face.
Reason (R): For a ray falling normally on the first face of a prism, the angle of incidence at the second refracting face is equal to the angle of the prism.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Geometry of a prism: r₁ + r₂ = A; total internal reflection when the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle
solution.explanation: Normal incidence means r₁ = 0, so r₂ = A = 60° (R true). The critical angle for n = 1.5 is sin⁻¹(2/3) ≈ 42°. Since 60° > 42°, the ray is totally internally reflected at the second face and does not emerge from it (A false).
steps: 60° > C → total internal reflection → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false because the ray is totally reflected at the second face; R is a correct geometrical result.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', total internal reflection; refraction through a prism
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A real object is placed on the principal axis of a thin convex lens of focal length 20 cm, at the distance from the lens given in List-I. Match each case with the image in List-II.

List-I:
A. 10 cm
B. 30 cm
C. 40 cm
D. 60 cm

List-II:
I. Real, 30 cm from the lens on the other side
II. Real, 40 cm from the lens on the other side
III. Virtual, 20 cm from the lens on the same side as the object
IV. Real, 60 cm from the lens on the other side

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Thin lens formula 1/v − 1/u = 1/f
solution.why_others_wrong: A-III, B-I, D-IV swaps the images for 30 cm and 60 cm (object and image distances are interchangeable, but not equal). A-IV/B-III makes the object inside f give a real image. C-I/D-II swaps the 2f case with the 60 cm case.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', thin lens formula
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-III, B-IV, C-II, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about thin lenses are correct?

(a) A thin equiconvex lens of glass of refractive index 1.5 has a focal length equal to the radius of curvature of its surfaces.
(b) A thin plano-convex lens of glass of refractive index 1.5 has a focal length equal to twice the radius of curvature of its curved surface.
(c) If such an equiconvex lens is immersed in a liquid of refractive index 1.5, it neither converges nor diverges light.
(d) A thin concave lens can form a real image of a real object.
(e) A thin convex lens forms a virtual image of a real object placed between its focus and its optical centre.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Lens maker's formula; image formation by thin lenses
solution.explanation: Equiconvex: 1/f = 0.5 × 2/R → f = R (a true). Plano-convex: 1/f = 0.5/R → f = 2R (b true). In a liquid of the same index, n_rel − 1 = 0, so the power is zero (c true). A concave lens always forms a virtual image of a real object (d false). An object inside the focus of a convex lens gives a virtual, erect, magnified image (e true).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (d) include a false statement; the other two options each leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Ray Optics and Optical Instruments', refraction by a lens; lens maker's formula

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Taking Planck's constant h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the energy of a photon of frequency 5.0 × 10¹⁴ Hz is:

solution.concept: Photon energy E = hν
solution.explanation: Each photon of radiation of frequency ν carries energy hν.
solution.why_others_wrong: 1.3 × 10⁻⁴⁸ J divides h by ν. 3.3 × 10⁻²⁰ J slips a power of ten. 2.1 × 10⁻¹⁹ J writes the energy in eV (2.1 eV) with the wrong unit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', photoelectric effect - Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: The threshold frequency for photoelectric emission from a metal is 1.0 × 10¹⁵ Hz. Light of frequency 1.5 × 10¹⁵ Hz falls on it. Taking h = 4.14 × 10⁻¹⁵ eV s, the maximum kinetic energy of the emitted photoelectrons is about:

solution.concept: Einstein's photoelectric equation: K_max = h(ν − ν₀)
solution.explanation: The work function is hν₀; the rest of the photon energy appears as the maximum kinetic energy.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6.21 eV is the whole photon energy hν. 4.14 eV is the work function hν₀. 10.35 eV adds the two frequencies.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: According to the values of work function listed in NCERT, which one of the following metals has the HIGHEST work function?

solution.concept: Work function of metals
solution.explanation: NCERT's table lists caesium about 2.14 eV, sodium about 2.75 eV, copper about 4.65 eV and platinum about 5.65 eV; platinum has the largest value of these.
steps: Cs ≈ 2.14 eV < Na ≈ 2.75 eV < Cu ≈ 4.65 eV < Pt ≈ 5.65 eV
solution.why_others_wrong: Caesium has the lowest work function of the common metals (it emits even with visible light). Sodium and copper lie between caesium and platinum.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', electron emission (Table: work functions of some metals)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Photons of energy 4.0 eV eject photoelectrons of maximum kinetic energy 1.5 eV from metal A. Metal B has a work function twice that of metal A. When photons of energy 6.0 eV fall on metal B, the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is:

solution.concept: Einstein's equation K_max = hν − φ₀
solution.explanation: First find the work function of A from the given data, double it for B, and then apply the equation again.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.5 eV uses the work function of A for metal B. 4.5 eV subtracts the kinetic energy from A instead of a work function. 6.0 eV exceeds 5.0 eV, so emission does occur.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: A nucleus at rest breaks up into two fragments whose masses are in the ratio 1 : 2, the fragments flying apart with speeds much smaller than that of light. The ratio of the de Broglie wavelengths of the two fragments is:

solution.concept: Conservation of momentum; de Broglie wavelength λ = h/p
solution.explanation: The total momentum is zero before the break-up, so the two fragments have equal and opposite momenta. Since λ = h/p depends only on the magnitude of the momentum, the wavelengths are equal.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2 : 1 and 1 : 2 make λ depend on mass alone (as if the speeds were equal). √2 : 1 assumes equal kinetic energies.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', wave nature of matter

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The work function of a metal does not depend on the nature of its surface.
Statement II: Electrons can be emitted from a metal surface by heating it suitably (thermionic emission) or by applying a very strong electric field (field emission).

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Work function and modes of electron emission
solution.explanation: NCERT states that the work function depends on the properties of the metal and the nature of its surface, so Statement I is false. Thermionic emission, field emission and photoelectric emission are the three ways listed by NCERT of supplying the minimum energy for electron emission (Statement II true).
steps: Work function depends on the metal and its surface → I false
Thermionic and field emission are valid modes → II true
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement I is false (surface condition matters); Statement II is true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', electron emission
solution.final_answer: Option D: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): For light of a frequency above the threshold frequency, photoelectric emission from a metal stops when the intensity of the light is reduced below a certain minimum value.
Reason (R): Photoelectric emission does not occur if the frequency of the incident light is below the threshold frequency, however intense the light may be.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Dependence of photoelectric emission on intensity and frequency
solution.explanation: Above the threshold, each photon can eject an electron, so even very dim light causes emission; lowering the intensity only reduces the number of electrons emitted per second (A false). Below the threshold, no photon has enough energy, so there is no emission at any intensity (R true).
steps: Above threshold: emission at any intensity; photocurrent ∝ intensity → A false
Below threshold: no emission at any intensity → R true
solution.why_others_wrong: A is false (there is no minimum intensity), while R is a correct NCERT observation.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', experimental study of photoelectric effect
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Photons of energy 3.0 eV fall on a metal of work function 2.2 eV. The fastest photoelectrons enter a uniform magnetic field of 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ T moving at right angles to it. Taking the electron mass as 9.0 × 10⁻³¹ kg and e = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the radius of their circular path is:

solution.concept: K_max = hν − φ₀; radius in a magnetic field r = p/(eB) = √(2mK)/(eB)
solution.explanation: The maximum kinetic energy is 0.8 eV. Converting to joules gives the momentum, and the radius follows from r = p/(eB).
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.1 cm uses p = √(mK), missing the factor 2. 5.8 cm takes the whole photon energy as kinetic energy. 1.5 cm halves the radius.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', Einstein's photoelectric equation; Class 12 Physics, 'Moving Charges and Magnetism', motion in a magnetic field

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text: Photons of energy 4.5 eV fall on the emitter of a photocell, whose work function is 2.0 eV. The collector is kept at a potential of −1.0 V with respect to the emitter. The maximum kinetic energy with which photoelectrons reach the collector is:

options.text: zero, since the collector is negative

solution.concept: Einstein's equation; work done against a retarding potential
solution.explanation: Electrons leave the emitter with at most 2.5 eV. Moving to a collector 1.0 V lower in potential, each electron loses 1.0 eV of kinetic energy. Since 1.0 V is less than the stopping potential (2.5 V), the fastest electrons still arrive.
steps: Loss in retarding field = e × 1.0 V = 1.0 eV
solution.why_others_wrong: 3.5 eV adds the energy of the retarding field instead of subtracting it. 2.5 eV ignores the retarding potential. The current becomes zero only when the retarding potential reaches the stopping potential, 2.5 V.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', effect of potential on photoelectric current

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Dual Nature of Matter and Radiation
questions.question_text:
According to the photon picture of electromagnetic radiation, which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Photons are electrically neutral and are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.
(b) A photon of frequency ν has energy hν and momentum of magnitude hν/c.
(c) Increasing the intensity of light of a given wavelength increases the number of photons crossing unit area per unit time, not the energy of each photon.
(d) The energy of each photon in a beam increases when the intensity of the beam is increased.
(e) All photons travel with the same speed c in vacuum, whatever their frequency.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Particle nature of light: the photon
solution.explanation: Photons carry no charge (a true). E = hν and p = hν/c (b true). Intensity is set by the photon flux; the energy per photon depends only on frequency (c true, d false). Every photon moves at c in vacuum (e true).
steps: (d) false: photon energy depends on ν only
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (d) include a false statement; the remaining options each leave out a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Dual Nature of Radiation and Matter', particle nature of light: the photon

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The mass defect of the ¹⁶₈O nucleus is 0.1374 u. Taking 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², the binding energy per nucleon of ¹⁶O is about:

solution.concept: B.E. = Δm c²; binding energy per nucleon = B.E./A
solution.explanation: The total binding energy is the energy equivalent of the mass defect; dividing by the number of nucleons (A = 16) gives the binding energy per nucleon.
solution.why_others_wrong: 128 MeV is the total binding energy. 16 MeV divides by Z = 8 instead of A = 16. 0.0086 MeV divides the mass defect by A without converting to energy.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass-energy and nuclear binding energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the series of fusion reactions by which four hydrogen nuclei (with two electrons) are converted into one helium nucleus in the Sun, the total mass that disappears is about 0.0287 u. Taking 1 u = 931.5 MeV/c², the energy released is about:

solution.concept: Energy released in fusion Q = Δm c²
solution.explanation: The disappearing mass appears as energy at 931.5 MeV per u.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.0287 MeV forgets to convert u to MeV. 6.7 MeV is the energy per nucleon (26.7/4), not per reaction. 2.67 × 10³ MeV slips two powers of ten.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', nuclear fusion - energy generation in stars

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: de Broglie's explanation of Bohr's quantisation of angular momentum states that, for an electron in a stationary orbit of radius r_n,

options.text: the radius of the orbit equals a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths: r_n = nλ
the circumference of the orbit contains a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths: 2πr_n = nλ
the circumference of the orbit equals half a de Broglie wavelength
the de Broglie wavelength of the electron is the same in every orbit

solution.concept: Electron as a standing wave on its orbit
solution.explanation: A stationary orbit is one in which the electron wave forms a standing wave, so the circumference must be an integral number of wavelengths. With λ = h/(mv), 2πr_n = nh/(mv) gives mvr_n = nh/2π, Bohr's condition.
solution.why_others_wrong: r_n = nλ would give mvr = nh, not nh/2π. Half a wavelength cannot form a standing wave round a closed loop. The speed, and hence λ, differs from orbit to orbit.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', de Broglie's explanation of Bohr's second postulate of quantisation
solution.final_answer: Option B: the circumference of the orbit contains a whole number of de Broglie wavelengths: 2πr_n = nλ

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The Bohr model can be applied to hydrogen-like ions such as He⁺ and Li²⁺, which have a single electron.
Statement II: The Bohr model explains the relative intensities of the lines in the hydrogen spectrum.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Scope and limitations of the Bohr model
solution.explanation: The model treats a single electron moving round a nucleus of charge Ze, so it applies to hydrogen-like ions (Statement I true). NCERT lists among its limitations that it cannot explain the relative intensities of the spectral lines (Statement II false).
steps: Single electron + nucleus Ze → applies to He⁺, Li²⁺ → I true
Relative intensities not explained → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II states the opposite of a limitation listed in NCERT.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom (limitations)
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The binding energy of the ⁴₂He nucleus is 28.3 MeV and that of the deuteron (²₁H) is 2.22 MeV. The minimum energy needed to split a ⁴He nucleus into two deuterons is about:

solution.concept: Energy balance with binding energies: energy needed = B.E.(initial) − Σ B.E.(products)
solution.explanation: Splitting ⁴He completely would need 28.3 MeV, but forming two deuterons gives back their binding energy, 2 × 2.22 MeV.
solution.why_others_wrong: 26.1 MeV subtracts the binding energy of only one deuteron. 32.7 MeV adds the deuterons' binding energy instead of subtracting it. 28.3 MeV is the energy to separate ⁴He into four free nucleons.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', mass-energy and nuclear binding energy

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In the Bohr model the energy levels of a hydrogen-like ion are E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV. A photon emitted when a He⁺ ion (Z = 2) makes the transition n = 2 → n = 1 is absorbed by a hydrogen atom in its ground state. The kinetic energy of the electron ejected from the hydrogen atom is:

options.text: No electron is ejected, since the photon has only 10.2 eV

solution.concept: Photon energy hν = E_i − E_f; ionisation of hydrogen needs 13.6 eV
solution.explanation: The He⁺ photon has energy 13.6 × 4 × (1 − ¼) = 40.8 eV, much more than the 13.6 eV needed to ionise ground-state hydrogen; the excess is the kinetic energy of the ejected electron.
solution.why_others_wrong: 40.8 eV forgets the ionisation energy of hydrogen. 54.4 eV is the ionisation energy of He⁺. 10.2 eV is the 2 → 1 photon of hydrogen, not of He⁺ (it misses the Z² factor).
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom; energy levels

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A hydrogen atom emits a photon of energy 2.55 eV. Using E_n = −13.6/n² eV, the transition responsible is:

solution.concept: Photon energy equals the difference of two energy levels
solution.explanation: The levels are −13.6, −3.40, −1.51, −0.85 eV for n = 1 to 4. Only the pair n = 4 and n = 2 differ by 2.55 eV.
solution.why_others_wrong: 3 → 2 gives 1.89 eV (Hα). 4 → 3 gives 0.66 eV. 2 → 1 gives 10.2 eV.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', the line spectra of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): In the Bohr model, the electron in a hydrogen atom can revolve round the nucleus in a stable orbit of any radius.
Reason (R): In the Bohr model, the angular momentum of the electron in a stationary orbit is an integral multiple of h/2π.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Bohr's postulates: quantised angular momentum leads to discrete orbits r_n ∝ n²
solution.explanation: Bohr allowed only those orbits for which mvr = nh/2π (R true). This restricts the radii to the discrete values r_n = n²a₀, so orbits of arbitrary radius are not allowed (A false).
steps: r_n = n² × 0.53 Å only → A false
solution.why_others_wrong: A contradicts the very quantisation stated in R; R is true.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom
solution.final_answer: Option D: A is false but R is true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Using E_n = −13.6/n² eV for the hydrogen atom, match each transition in List-I with the energy of the photon emitted in List-II.

List-I:
A. n = 2 → n = 1
B. n = 3 → n = 2
C. n = 3 → n = 1
D. n = ∞ → n = 1 (series limit of the Lyman series)

List-II:
I. 12.09 eV
II. 1.89 eV
III. 13.6 eV
IV. 10.2 eV

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Photon energy hν = E_i − E_f
solution.explanation: E₁ = −13.6, E₂ = −3.40, E₃ = −1.51 eV. The differences give the photon energies.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-I/C-IV swaps the 2 → 1 and 3 → 1 lines. C-III/D-I swaps 3 → 1 with the series limit. B-I/C-II swaps the Balmer and Lyman lines from n = 3.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', the line spectra of the hydrogen atom
solution.final_answer: Option B: A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A nuclear reactor generates thermal power at the rate of 320 MW by the fission of ²³⁵U, each fission releasing 200 MeV. Taking 1 MeV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹³ J and Avogadro's number as 6.0 × 10²³ mol⁻¹, the mass of ²³⁵U consumed in one hour is about:

solution.concept: Fission rate = power/energy per fission; mass = (number of nuclei/N_A) × molar mass
solution.explanation: First find the number of fissions per second, then the number in one hour, and convert that number of ²³⁵U nuclei to grams using 235 g per mole.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.24 g is the mass consumed in one minute. 340 g is the mass consumed in a day. 1.4 g slips a power of ten.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Nuclei', nuclear energy - fission

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A hydrogen-like ion in its ground state has an ionisation energy of 122.4 eV. In the Bohr model, the energy levels are E_n = −13.6 Z²/n² eV and the orbit radii are r_n = (0.53 Å) n²/Z. The radius of the ground-state orbit of this ion is about:

solution.concept: Hydrogen-like ions: E ∝ Z², r ∝ 1/Z
solution.explanation: The ionisation energy from the ground state is 13.6 Z² eV, which gives Z. The radius then scales as 1/Z.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.059 Å divides by Z² instead of Z. 1.59 Å multiplies by Z. 0.53 Å is the hydrogen value, ignoring Z.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
A hydrogen atom is in the state n = 3 of the Bohr model (E_n = −13.6/n² eV, r_n = 0.53 n² Å). Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Its total energy is about −1.51 eV.
(b) The radius of the electron's orbit is about 4.77 Å.
(c) In returning to the ground state, possibly in steps, it can emit photons of three different wavelengths.
(d) The longest wavelength it can emit belongs to the Balmer series.
(e) The angular momentum of the electron is h/π.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Energy, radius and angular momentum in the Bohr model; possible transitions
solution.explanation: E₃ = −13.6/9 ≈ −1.51 eV (a true). r₃ = 9 × 0.53 ≈ 4.77 Å (b true). Possible downward transitions: 3 → 1, 3 → 2 and 2 → 1, i.e. three wavelengths (c true). The smallest energy jump, 3 → 2 (1.89 eV), gives the longest wavelength and ends on n = 2, a Balmer line (d true). L = 3h/2π, not h/π (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options containing (e) include a false statement; the others leave out at least one true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Atoms', Bohr model of the hydrogen atom; the line spectra of the hydrogen atom

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a doped silicon sample at thermal equilibrium, the electron concentration is 4 × 10²² m⁻³ and the hole concentration is 1 × 10¹⁰ m⁻³. The intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon at this temperature is:

solution.concept: Mass-action law: n_e n_h = n_i²
solution.explanation: In thermal equilibrium the product of the electron and hole concentrations equals the square of the intrinsic concentration, whatever the doping.
solution.why_others_wrong: 4 × 10³² m⁻³ is n_i², not n_i. 4 × 10¹² m⁻³ is the ratio n_e/n_h. 2 × 10³² m⁻³ halves the product instead of taking its square root.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode of breakdown voltage 8.0 V is operating in its breakdown region and carries a current of 25 mA. The power dissipated in the Zener diode is:

solution.concept: Power P = VI
solution.explanation: In breakdown, the voltage across the Zener is its breakdown voltage, so the power is V_Z I_Z.
solution.why_others_wrong: 200 W leaves the current in mA. 0.32 W divides V² by an assumed 200 Ω, which has no basis here. 2.0 W slips a power of ten.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', Zener diode

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Silicon is doped with phosphorus (a pentavalent impurity). After each phosphorus atom has donated its fifth electron to the conduction band, the phosphorus atom in the crystal becomes:

options.text: a mobile positive charge carrier, i.e. a hole
a neutral atom that can move through the crystal

solution.concept: Donor impurities in n-type semiconductors
solution.explanation: Four of the five valence electrons of phosphorus form covalent bonds with neighbouring silicon atoms; the fifth is loosely bound and is easily freed. Having lost one electron, the donor atom is left as a positive ion, fixed in the crystal lattice.
steps: Donor gives up its fifth electron
Donor becomes a positive ion, bound in the lattice (immobile)
solution.why_others_wrong: A hole is a vacancy in a covalent bond, not an ionised donor. A negative ion forms from an acceptor (trivalent) impurity. The donor atom is part of the lattice and cannot move.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor - n-type
solution.final_answer: Option D: an immobile positive ion

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each term related to semiconductors in List-I with its description in List-II.

List-I:
A. Doping
B. Hole
C. Depletion region
D. Barrier potential

List-II:
I. The region near a p-n junction that has been emptied of mobile charge carriers
II. A vacancy in a covalent bond, which behaves as a positive charge carrier
III. The potential difference across a p-n junction that opposes further diffusion of majority carriers
IV. Adding a small, controlled amount of a suitable impurity to a pure semiconductor

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Basic terms of semiconductor physics
solution.explanation: Doping adds impurity atoms to change the conductivity. A hole is the vacancy left when an electron leaves a bond. Diffusion across a junction leaves a layer of fixed ions with no mobile carriers (depletion region), and the field of these ions sets up the barrier potential.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II/B-IV swaps doping and hole. C-III/D-I swaps the depletion region and the barrier potential. B-I/C-II swaps the hole and the depletion region.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', intrinsic and extrinsic semiconductors; p-n junction formation
solution.final_answer: Option A: A-IV, B-II, C-I, D-III

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: Four photodiodes are made of semiconductors with the band gaps listed below. Light of wavelength 600 nm falls on each. Taking hc = 1240 eV nm, the photodiode that will respond to this light is the one with a band gap of:

solution.concept: A photodiode responds only to photons with energy hν ≥ E_g
solution.explanation: Electron–hole pairs are generated only if each photon can lift an electron across the band gap.
steps: Only E_g = 1.8 eV is less than 2.07 eV
solution.why_others_wrong: Band gaps of 2.2 eV, 2.5 eV and 3.0 eV are all larger than the photon energy (2.07 eV), so no electron–hole pairs are produced in them.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices - photodiode

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A 9 V battery and a 3 V battery (both ideal) are connected in a single series loop with a 2 kΩ resistor and an ideal junction diode. The batteries oppose each other (positive terminal of one joined to the positive terminal of the other), and the diode is connected so that it is forward biased by the net emf. The current in the loop is:

solution.concept: Ideal diode: zero resistance when forward biased; opposing emfs subtract
solution.explanation: The net emf is 9 − 3 = 6 V, in the direction of the 9 V battery. The diode conducts in that direction, so it acts as a plain wire and the 2 kΩ resistor alone limits the current.
solution.why_others_wrong: 6 mA adds the emfs, though they oppose each other. 4.5 mA ignores the 3 V battery. Zero would apply only if the diode were reverse biased by the net emf.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction diode under forward bias

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): There are practically no mobile charge carriers in the depletion region of an unbiased p-n junction.
Reason (R): The energy band gap of germanium is smaller than that of silicon.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Depletion region; band gaps of Si and Ge
solution.explanation: Electrons and holes diffusing across the junction recombine, leaving behind only fixed donor and acceptor ions near the junction (A true). The band gap of Ge (about 0.7 eV) is smaller than that of Si (about 1.1 eV), so R is true, but it says nothing about why the depletion region lacks mobile carriers.
steps: Diffusion + recombination → only immobile ions near the junction → A true
E_g(Ge) ≈ 0.7 eV < E_g(Si) ≈ 1.1 eV → R true
solution.why_others_wrong: R is a true but unrelated property of the two materials, so it is not the explanation of A.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', p-n junction formation; classification of metals, conductors and semiconductors
solution.final_answer: Option B: Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: The reverse breakdown voltages of light emitting diodes are very low, typically around 5 V.
Statement II: The light emitted by an LED is thermal radiation from its junction, which is heated by the current.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Light emitting diode
solution.explanation: NCERT notes that LEDs have very low reverse breakdown voltages, typically about 5 V, so care is needed to avoid reverse voltages (Statement I true). The light comes from the recombination of electrons and holes near the junction under forward bias, the energy being released as photons; it is not thermal radiation (Statement II false).
steps: LED reverse breakdown ≈ 5 V → I true
Emission from electron–hole recombination → II false
solution.why_others_wrong: Statement II confuses an LED with an incandescent lamp.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', optoelectronic junction devices - light emitting diode
solution.final_answer: Option C: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each combination of logic gates in List-I with the single gate it is equivalent to in List-II.

List-I:
A. A two-input NAND gate with both its inputs joined together
B. Each of the inputs A and B passed through a NOT gate, and the two outputs fed to a NAND gate
C. An OR gate followed by a NOT gate
D. Each of the inputs A and B passed through a NOT gate, and the two outputs fed to a NOR gate

List-II:
I. OR
II. AND
III. NOT
IV. NOR

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Truth tables of NOT, NAND, NOR; inverting the inputs
solution.explanation: NAND with joined inputs gives NOT(A·A) = Ā. NAND of Ā and B̄ is NOT(Ā·B̄), which is 1 unless both A and B are 0, i.e. OR. OR followed by NOT is NOR. NOR of Ā and B̄ is 1 only when Ā = B̄ = 0, i.e. A = B = 1, which is AND.
solution.why_others_wrong: B-II/D-I swaps the inverted-input NAND and NOR. A-IV/C-III swaps the joined-input NAND and OR + NOT. C-II/D-IV gives OR + NOT the output of AND.
solution.ncert_reference: Logic gates (NMC syllabus: OR, AND, NOT, NAND and NOR)
solution.final_answer: Option D: A-III, B-I, C-IV, D-II

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about the Zener diode are correct?

(a) Under forward bias, a Zener diode behaves like an ordinary junction diode.
(b) Zener breakdown occurs because the very high electric field across the thin depletion layer pulls valence electrons out of the host atoms.
(c) In the breakdown region, the voltage across a Zener diode stays almost constant over a wide range of current.
(d) A Zener diode used as a voltage regulator is connected in forward bias.
(e) A Zener diode has lightly doped p- and n-regions.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Zener diode: heavy doping, thin depletion layer, field-induced breakdown
solution.explanation: In forward bias the Zener conducts like any p-n diode (a true). Heavy doping gives a very thin depletion layer, so a few volts of reverse bias produce a field of about 5 × 10⁶ V/m, which pulls valence electrons free (b true). In breakdown the voltage is nearly constant while the current changes greatly (c true). As a regulator it is reverse biased (d false). Both sides are heavily, not lightly, doped (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (c) only misses the true statement (b); options with (d) or (e) contain a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Zener diode (NMC syllabus: I-V characteristics and voltage regulator)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A Zener diode of breakdown voltage 6.0 V is connected through a 300 Ω series resistor to a 12 V DC supply, and a load resistor R_L is connected across the Zener diode. Treating the Zener as drawing current only when the voltage across it would otherwise exceed 6.0 V, the smallest value of R_L for which the load voltage remains 6.0 V is:

options.text: There is no lower limit; any load gives 6.0 V

solution.concept: Zener regulator: I_series = (V_in − V_Z)/R_s is shared by the Zener and the load
solution.explanation: While the Zener regulates, the series resistor has 12 − 6 = 6 V across it, so it carries 20 mA. The load can take at most all of this current (Zener current falling to zero), which fixes the smallest load resistance.
solution.why_others_wrong: 600 Ω divides the supply voltage, not the load voltage, by 20 mA. 150 Ω uses the supply voltage across the series resistor (40 mA). A very small load would draw so much current that the Zener leaves breakdown.
solution.ncert_reference: Zener diode as a voltage regulator (NMC syllabus)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: The barrier potential of an unbiased p-n junction is 0.70 V. The junction is now forward biased by 0.30 V. An electron in the n-region approaches the junction with a kinetic energy of 0.60 eV. Treating the effective barrier as the only obstacle, the kinetic energy with which it enters the p-region is:

solution.concept: Forward bias lowers the barrier height to V₀ − V
solution.explanation: Forward bias opposes the built-in potential, so the effective barrier is 0.70 − 0.30 = 0.40 V. The electron loses 0.40 eV in climbing it.
solution.why_others_wrong: 'Cannot cross' uses the unbiased barrier of 0.70 V. 0.90 eV adds the bias voltage to the kinetic energy. 0.60 eV ignores the barrier altogether.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', semiconductor diode - p-n junction diode under forward bias

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled Assertion (A) and the other is labelled Reason (R).

Assertion (A): At room temperature, doping pure silicon with a donor impurity at a concentration of only one part per million increases its conductivity enormously.
Reason (R): Each donor atom provides a free electron, and the donor concentration (about 10²² m⁻³) is millions of times larger than the intrinsic carrier concentration of silicon (about 10¹⁶ m⁻³).

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

solution.concept: Extrinsic semiconductors: carrier concentration set by doping
solution.explanation: Silicon has about 5 × 10²⁸ atoms per m³, so 1 ppm of donors gives about 5 × 10²² free electrons per m³, compared with an intrinsic concentration of about 1.5 × 10¹⁶ m⁻³. The number of carriers, and hence the conductivity, rises by a factor of about a million. R gives exactly this reason.
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are true, and the huge increase in the number of free carriers is the reason for the rise in conductivity.
solution.ncert_reference: Class 12 Physics, 'Semiconductor Electronics: Materials, Devices and Simple Circuits', extrinsic semiconductor
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Inputs A and B are fed both to an AND gate and to a NOR gate, and the outputs of these two gates are fed to an OR gate, whose output is Y. Which of the following statements are correct?

(a) Y = 1 when A = 0 and B = 0.
(b) Y = 0 when A = 0 and B = 1.
(c) Y = 1 when A = 1 and B = 1.
(d) Y = 1 when A = 1 and B = 0.
(e) The circuit is equivalent to a NOR gate followed by a NOT gate.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Truth tables of AND, NOR and OR
solution.explanation: AND gives 1 only for (1, 1); NOR gives 1 only for (0, 0). Their OR is therefore 1 for (0, 0) and (1, 1) and 0 for (0, 1) and (1, 0): Y = 1 when the inputs are equal. A NOR followed by a NOT is an OR gate (0, 1, 1, 1), which is different.
solution.why_others_wrong: (a) and (c) only misses (b); options with (d) or (e) contain a false statement.
solution.ncert_reference: Logic gates (NMC syllabus: OR, AND, NOT, NAND and NOR)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: In a resonance-tube experiment with a tuning fork of frequency 480 Hz, the first resonance is obtained when the air column is 17.5 cm long. Neglecting the end correction, the speed of sound in air is:

solution.concept: First resonance of a tube closed at one end: l = λ/4
solution.explanation: At the first resonance the air column holds a quarter wavelength (node at the water surface, antinode at the open end), so λ = 4l and v = fλ.
solution.why_others_wrong: 168 m/s uses λ = 2l (an open pipe). 84 m/s uses λ = l. 672 m/s uses λ = 8l.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: speed of sound in air at room temperature using a resonance tube

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Given below are two statements:

Statement I: When the jaws of a vernier calipers are closed, if the zero of the vernier scale lies to the left of the zero of the main scale, the instrument has a negative zero error.
Statement II: The zero correction is equal in magnitude and opposite in sign to the zero error.

In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:

options.text: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.
Both Statement I and Statement II are false.
Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
Statement I is false but Statement II is true.

solution.concept: Zero error and zero correction
solution.explanation: With the zero of the vernier to the left of the main-scale zero, every reading is too small, so the zero error is negative (Statement I true). The correction to be added is the zero error with its sign reversed: corrected reading = observed reading − zero error (Statement II true).
steps: Vernier zero left of main zero → readings too small → negative zero error → I true
solution.why_others_wrong: Both statements are correct, so the options calling either one false are wrong.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: vernier calipers
solution.final_answer: Option A: Both Statement I and Statement II are true.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A screw gauge has a pitch of 1 mm and 100 divisions on its circular scale. With the studs in contact, the zero of the circular scale is 3 divisions above the reference line (a negative zero error). When a metal sheet is placed between the studs, the main-scale reading is 2 mm and the 45th circular division is on the reference line. The corrected thickness of the sheet is:

solution.concept: Least count = pitch/number of divisions; corrected reading = observed reading − zero error
solution.explanation: The least count is 0.01 mm. A circular-scale zero above the reference line means the reading is short of zero by 3 divisions: zero error = −0.03 mm. Subtracting a negative zero error adds 0.03 mm.
solution.why_others_wrong: 2.42 mm subtracts 0.03 mm, treating the error as positive. 2.45 mm ignores the zero error. 2.75 mm adds 30 divisions instead of 3.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: screw gauge (thickness of a sheet)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: To find the refractive index of a glass slab with a travelling microscope, the microscope is focused in turn on: (i) a mark on the table, reading 2.215 cm; (ii) the same mark seen through the slab placed over it, reading 2.715 cm; (iii) chalk dust sprinkled on the top surface of the slab, reading 3.715 cm. The refractive index of the glass is:

solution.concept: n = real thickness/apparent thickness
solution.explanation: The real thickness is the distance from the mark to the top surface, R₃ − R₁. The apparent thickness is from the raised image of the mark to the top surface, R₃ − R₂.
solution.why_others_wrong: 0.50 is the normal shift divided by the apparent thickness. 3.00 divides the real thickness by the normal shift (R₂ − R₁). 1.33 is the refractive index of water, not obtained from these readings.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: refractive index of a glass slab using a travelling microscope

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Match each experiment in List-I with a precaution that NCERT-based laboratory practice requires for it (List-II).

List-I:
A. Simple pendulum
B. Coefficient of viscosity by terminal velocity
C. Surface tension by capillary rise
D. Young's modulus by Searle's apparatus

List-II:
I. Remove kinks from the wire by first hanging a dead load on it
II. Start timing the ball only after it has fallen some distance through the liquid
III. Keep the angular amplitude of the oscillations small
IV. Clean the capillary tube thoroughly and hold it vertical

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Precautions in laboratory experiments
solution.explanation: The pendulum formula assumes small oscillations. Stokes' law with v constant applies only after the ball reaches terminal velocity. Grease or tilt spoils the capillary rise. A dead load straightens the wire before extensions are measured.
solution.why_others_wrong: A-II/B-III swaps the pendulum and viscosity precautions. C-I/D-IV swaps the capillary and Searle's precautions. B-IV/C-II swaps the viscosity and capillary precautions.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: simple pendulum; viscosity; surface tension; Young's modulus
solution.final_answer: Option C: A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text: A calorimeter contains 50 g of water at 20 °C. Then 50 g of water at 60 °C is poured in, and after stirring the steady temperature is 36 °C. Neglecting heat losses to the surroundings, the water equivalent of the calorimeter (with its stirrer) is:

solution.concept: Principle of calorimetry: heat lost by hot water = heat gained by cold water + calorimeter
solution.explanation: The hot water cools by 24 °C. The cold water and the calorimeter (taken as W grams of water) both warm by 16 °C.
steps: Heat lost = 50 × (60 − 36) = 1200 (in g °C, specific heat of water cancels)
solution.why_others_wrong: 75 g is the total (water + calorimeter), not the calorimeter alone. 50 g assumes equal temperature changes for the cold side. 10 g has no basis in the heat balance.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: specific heat capacity by the method of mixtures

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question_text:
Which of the following statements about vernier calipers and screw gauges are correct?

(a) The least count of a vernier calipers equals one main-scale division minus one vernier-scale division.
(b) A positive zero error is subtracted from the observed reading to obtain the corrected reading.
(c) A screw gauge of pitch 1 mm with 100 divisions on its circular scale has a least count of 0.01 mm.
(d) If, with the studs of a screw gauge in contact, the zero of the circular scale lies below the reference line, the zero error is positive.
(e) For a vernier calipers with a negative zero error, the magnitude of the zero error is subtracted from the observed reading.

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

solution.concept: Least count and zero error of vernier calipers and screw gauge
solution.explanation: LC = 1 MSD − 1 VSD (a true). Corrected = observed − zero error, so a positive error is subtracted (b true). LC = pitch/divisions = 0.01 mm (c true). With the circular zero below the reference line, the screw reads a positive value when it should read zero (d true). With a negative zero error, subtracting a negative number means adding its magnitude (e false).
solution.why_others_wrong: Options with (e) include a false statement; (a), (b) and (c) only and (b), (c) and (d) only each miss a true statement.
solution.ncert_reference: NMC syllabus, Experimental Skills: vernier calipers; screw gauge
